<section begin="correction-177a" />Rem. According to the prevailing view, this strengthening of the first radical is merely intended to give the bi-literal stem at least<section end="correction-177a" /> <section begin="correction-177b" />a tri-literal appearance. (Possibly aided by the analogy of verbs {{GHGheb|text=פ״ן}}, as {{nowrap|P. Haupt}} has suggested to me in conversation.) But cf. Kautzsch, ‘Die sog. aramaisierenden Formen der Verba {{GHGheb|text=ע״ע}} im Hebr.’ in {{GHGcite|title=Oriental. Studien zum 70. Geburtstag {{nowrap|Th. Nöldekes}}}}, 1906, p. 771 ff. It is there shown (1) that the sharpening of the 1st radical often serves to emphasize a particular meaning (cf. {{GHGheb|text=יִגָּר}}, but {{GHGheb|text=יְגֹרֵ֫הוּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָחֵל}} and {{GHGheb|text=יַחֵל}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִסֹּב}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָסֹב}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִשֹּׁם}} and {{GHGheb|text=תֵּשַׁם}}), and elsewhere no doubt to dissimilate the vowels (as {{GHGheb|text=יִגָּר}}, {{GHGheb|text=יִדַּל}}, never {{GHGheb|text=יָגַר}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָדַל}}, &c.): (2) that the sharpening of the 1st radical often appears to be occasioned by the nature of the first letter of the stem, especially when it is a sibilant. Whether the masoretic pronunciation is based on an early tradition, or the Masora has arbitrarily adopted aramaizing forms to attain the above objects, must be left undecided.<section end="correction-177b" />
